rationale: A wins because it has the better fact discipline, not because it has the sexier nose. B's sharpest line, "A blood-pressure feature that needs a blood-pressure cuff to work," is the best single hook in either set, but then it carelessly asserts "a feature nobody has cleared" without that fact in the update. A keeps marking missing proof, especially "the user must supply names and dates — the fact block doesn't name them," which is what keeps a founder out of correction territory.
gaps_in_A: "Cuffless blood pressure is the next wearable battleground" overstates the category shift from one Whoop launch; it needs market proof before it becomes a trend claim.
"catch-up-and-leapfrog story" is a little too cute. ECG catch-up is grounded; "leapfrog" is not proven until Whoop shows BP accuracy, differentiation, or adoption.
Angles 1 and 4 both orbit the same spine: competitors already have ECG, so BP is the next fight. The altitude changes, but the raw story repeats.
A misses B's sharper consumer-accountability angle around a blood-pressure feature that still needs cuff calibration.
gaps_in_B: "a feature nobody has cleared" is invented. The update says Whoop's BP estimate is not diagnostic; it does not say no company has a cleared cuffless BP product.
"a company whose entire model is subscription rather than hardware margin" imports outside knowledge. The supplied fact is only that the features sit behind the most expensive membership tier.
"Health reporters are actively covering wearable-accuracy gaps" is an unsupported current-media claim. Maybe true, maybe useful, but it is not in the fact block.
The next step, "newsjack-detector," is a detour for a live launch. Pick the provable angle and run journalist-fit-check unless there is a separate breaking peg.
